claims.text: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy is equiatomic and has a single-phase BCC microstructure.
The untreated alloy has high strength.
The untreated alloy releases energy under impact.
The untreated alloy has very limited room-temperature ductility.
Adding approximately 2 at% Ti during synthesis will promote in situ nucleation of nanoscale ductile precipitates at grain boundaries.
The proposed processing can preserve a primarily BCC refractory matrix while maintaining a ductile-precipitate fraction below approximately 3%.
Nanoscale ductile grain-boundary precipitates facilitate grain-boundary sliding.
Nanoscale ductile grain-boundary precipitates promote a more homogeneous strain distribution.
The precipitate-mediated strain distribution delays localized crack initiation.
Nanoscale ductile regions blunt crack propagation during deformation.
Nanoscale ductile regions enhance room-temperature plastic flow.
Limiting the ductile regions to a low volume fraction prevents significant interruption of the high-strength matrix.
A low volume fraction of ductile regions preserves impact-induced energy-release characteristics.
The Ti-treated alloy will have at least a 10–20% increase in room-temperature uniform elongation relative to the untreated alloy.
The Ti-treated alloy will retain high-temperature strength within approximately 5–10% of the untreated baseline.
The Ti-treated alloy will retain impact-induced energy release within approximately 5–10% of the untreated baseline.
The proposed improvement is contingent on avoiding precipitate coarsening.
Increasing the ductile-phase fraction beyond approximately 3% may reduce high-temperature strength.
Increasing the ductile-phase fraction beyond approximately 3% may alter impact-induced energy release.
Precipitates smaller than 10 nm would constitute the intended nanoscale mediator.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis concerns preservation of impact-induced energy release, but the proposed Charpy or drop-weight measurement is described as impact energy absorption. Absorbed mechanical energy is not equivalent to chemically or physically released energy, so the experiment does not directly test the stated impact-energy-release outcome.
